newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Fazio says avge Italy CPI in 1996 at 3.8 pct.
newsitem.headline: Fazio says avge Italy CPI in 1996 at 3.8 pct.

text.p: Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio said the bank was closely watching domestic inflation figures and that in a few weeks data will show if CPI was heading in the right direction.
Fazio was speaking to reporters at the regular G10 meeting of central bank governors in Basle.
He also said Italian consumer price inflation in 1996 was averaging 3.8 percent.
"In a few weeks we will have a series of (CPI) data which will show us if we are going in the right direction. We are now averaging 3.8 pct," he said.
Fazio added that average 1997 inflation should be "below 3.0 percent."
The government's latest target is for average 1996 inflation of 3.9 percent and has set a goal of an average 2.5 percent for 1997.
Italian CPI fell to 2.6 percent year-on-year in November from an annual 3.0 percent in October and against 6.0 percent in November 1995. Inflation has been falling steadily all year.
Preliminary CPI data for December from 10 Italian cities is due out around December 20.
Fazio said that given the clear improvement on the inflation front, "what's been happening to market rates is substantially justified...The Treasury pays market rates and these rates have fallen."
Fazio made no direct reference to the central bank's 7.5 percent discount rate, referring only to market rates.
A Reuter survey of economists last week showed the Bank of Italy was mostly seen waiting until at least mid-December before trimming the discount rate by 50 basis points.

But several said a rate move at any moment would not be a surprise given the lira's recent strength following its return to Europe's exchange rate mechanism at a central rate of 990 per mark on November 24.
Fazio, referring to the lira's exchange rate, said, "you can see, (the lira) has stood up very well."
At 1300 GMT, the lira was quoted at 985.00/5.35 per mark.

On the European economy, he said "there are signs of a general recovery in 1997...(but) in Italy the situation is peculiar because since our economy grew more beforehand, it will follow on with some delay."
